text:
In nineteen fifty, Alan Turing asked whether machines can think, then swapped that question for a test. A judge trades typed messages with a hidden person and a hidden machine. If the judge can't tell which is which, the machine passes. He called it the imitation game. We call it the Turing test, and every chatbot since has been chasing it. Four years later, a demo made that goal look close.

In nineteen fifty-four, Georgetown and IBM showed a computer translating Russian into English. It knew two hundred and fifty words and six grammar rules, and translated about sixty hand-picked sentences. The papers loved it. One of its leaders predicted working translation in five years, perhaps three. Twelve years later, a government committee saw no prospect of useful machine translation, and the funding dried up. A polished demo is not a working system. And that same year, a tiny program at MIT showed a subtler trap.

Joseph Weizenbaum wrote Eliza, a program that played a therapist. Its whole trick: spot a phrase like I need, and hand it back as a question. There's no understanding in it at all. Yet people confided in it. Weizenbaum's own secretary asked him to leave the room. Seeing real understanding in a simple text trick is now called the Eliza effect. Meanwhile, the quiet counting kept paying off.
